<command>cd /work/tides && git status --short</command>
<command>cd /work/tides && git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U</command>
<command>cd /work/tides && git diff tides/heights.py</command>
<command>cd /work/tides && git log --oneline -5 main -- tides/heights.py</command>

The last one shows what the upstream commits (`4c19e07..b8d2a51`) changed in that file, so I can tell whether the two sides are compatible.

**What I'd do after reading the hunks:**

1. If the conflict is mechanical (both sides touch adjacent lines and the intents combine cleanly), I'd resolve it in `tides/heights.py`, removing the markers and keeping both intents. I'd then run `git add tides/heights.py`.
2. If the two sides disagree on behavior, such as different rounding rules or precision, I'd stop and ask you which wins instead of guessing.
3. I'd run the project's documented test command on the resolved result. It must pass before I commit.
4. I'd commit the merge with `git commit` (default merge message) and confirm `git status` is clean.
5. Because the resolution adds code the Codex review never saw, I'd tell you plainly that the review covered the branch before the merge, not the resolved result. If the resolution is more than trivial, I'd suggest a quick look at it.
6. Only after the merge is committed and tests pass would I clean up. That means `git worktree remove /work/tides-height-rounding` and `git worktree prune` from `/work/tides`, then `git branch -d feat/height-rounding`. I'd do this because this session made the worktree.

I would not run `git merge --abort` or `git reset` unless you ask.
